notable.name: Indigenous languages (Nahuatl, Maya, Zapotec, Mixtec, and dozens more)
notable.family: various — Uto-Aztecan, Mayan, Oto-Manguean, and other families
notable.note: 68 nationally recognized indigenous languages; federal road signage is Spanish-only, with limited regional bilingual exceptions (e.g. Spanish/Maya signage in parts of Yucatán)

terrainDescription.zh: 北部為沙漠地形（索諾拉、奇瓦瓦沙漠），中部為高原與馬德雷山脈，南部恰帕斯、猶加敦一帶轉為熱帶雨林，沿岸與農業平原分布各地；此處僅列全國通用特徵，各州地理差異極大，區域細節待日後擴充。
terrainDescription.en: Desert in the north (Sonoran, Chihuahuan), a mountainous central plateau (Sierra Madre ranges), tropical rainforest in the south (Chiapas, Yucatán), and coastal/agricultural land throughout. This covers only nationwide common features; regional/state-level variation is substantial and left for future expansion.

plate.color: design/background varies by state (32 federal entities), though a common national baseline format exists; this is a nationwide summary only, state-level plate design is out of scope here

roadInfra.bollardStyle: Not strongly documented as a distinct national style in sources checked this pass; yellow-and-black striped concrete speed bumps ("topes") are a much more distinctive and commonly-cited Mexican road feature than bollards specifically — flagging bollardStyle as low-confidence rather than inventing detail

utilityPole.transformerMount: Concrete poles are the most common type nationally, as in much of the rest of Latin America; wood poles also occur, more often in rural/southern areas

historicalContext.zh: 西班牙語因殖民歷史成為官方語言，但墨西哥境內原住民語言多樣性極高（官方承認68種語言），聯邦路牌僅使用西班牙語，猶加敦部分地區則有西班牙語／馬雅語雙語路牌的例外情況；墨西哥的道路標誌系統（八角形STOP/ALTO標誌、黃色菱形警示標誌）與美國MUTCD系統高度相近，是與中南美洲其他國家常見的維也納公約式標誌明顯不同之處。
historicalContext.en: Spanish became the official language through colonial history, but Mexico has exceptionally high indigenous linguistic diversity (68 officially recognized languages); federal road signage is Spanish-only, with an exception in parts of Yucatán where Spanish/Maya bilingual signage appears. Mexico's road-sign system (octagonal STOP/ALTO signs, yellow diamond warning signs) closely mirrors the US MUTCD system — a notable contrast with the Vienna-Convention-style signage common elsewhere in Latin America.
